vignette:
He is sixty-seven now, a widowed North American man who spent most of his adult life as a military medic, and he still tells the story like someone giving a careful field report: dates approximated, weather noted, sequence preserved. But as he talks, the order of events keeps getting interrupted by the force of what returns to him.

The collision happens more than a decade ago, after he has already left active service. He is driving home at dusk on a wet two-lane highway after visiting his wife's sister. He remembers the smell inside the truck-coffee gone cold in the cup holder, damp wool from his jacket, the faint medicinal odor of the first-aid kit he always keeps under the seat. He sees headlights drift over the center line and has just enough time to think, with a medic's detached clarity, This is going to be bad. Then there is a violent burst of sound and pressure, metal folding in on itself, glass spraying across his face, his chest pinned by the seat belt so hard he cannot draw a full breath.

What he remembers most clearly is not fear at first but training. He checks himself automatically: airway, bleeding, limbs. He tastes blood and feels heat in his left shoulder. The dashboard is crushed inward. One leg is trapped. Somewhere nearby another driver is screaming. He cannot tell if the sound is outside the truck or inside his own head. He tries to force the door and cannot. The smell of gasoline reaches him, and that is when panic overtakes procedure. He is no longer a medic assessing a scene; he is a man who believes he is about to burn alive in a machine he cannot escape.

He survives. Bystanders and paramedics extricate him. In the emergency department he drifts in and out, angry at being immobilized, angry at the questions, angry that his hands are shaking when he has spent years being the one who steadies other people. He tells himself, and everyone else, that he is lucky. He has seen worse. He has worked on young soldiers with catastrophic injuries and civilians torn apart on roadways. Compared to that, he says, this is manageable.

For a while, he lives as if that is true. His body heals faster than his mind. He returns to driving because he thinks avoidance is weakness. But every time headlights approach on a narrow road, his back tightens against the seat. If a car drifts even slightly, his hands clamp down so hard his knuckles ache. He begins taking longer routes to avoid highways, then insists he simply prefers back roads. At red lights he studies mirrors compulsively, calculating impact angles, exit paths, where he would drag an unconscious passenger if he had to. He keeps trauma shears and extra bandages in the glove compartment, then a tourniquet, then a fire extinguisher. He knows this is excessive, but preparedness has always been the way he makes the world feel survivable.

At night the collision returns without warning. In sleep he is trapped again, chest crushed, gasoline in his nose, unable to free his leg. He wakes soaked in sweat and already moving, sometimes halfway out of bed before he knows where he is. His wife used to place a hand on his shoulder and say his name until he came back. After she dies several years later from cancer, the nights become worse. There is no one there to orient him. He sleeps in short fragments in a recliner with the television on low because silence gives too much room for memory.

He does not like talking about emotion, but he describes living "keyed up." Sudden sounds-a dropped tool in the garage, a truck backfiring outside the grocery store-send a jolt through him so strong he feels embarrassed afterward. In crowds he scans constantly for hazards and exits. If he sees a wreck on the roadside, he cannot look away, yet afterward the rest of the day is gone to him. Images intrude while he is washing dishes or standing in line at the pharmacy: shattered windshield glass glittering on his lap, the smell of fuel, the certainty that he is about to die. He becomes irritable in ways he does not recognize as himself. He snaps at clerks, withdraws from friends from the service, declines invitations he used to accept. People describe him as private; he knows he is shrinking his life.

What troubles him most is the humiliation of being undone by a car crash after a career spent running toward emergencies. He compares himself harshly to the younger medic he once was. He says he should have handled it better, should have gotten over it by now, should be able to drive at night without rehearsing catastrophe. Yet as he speaks, it becomes clear that he is still living partly inside that cab at dusk, listening for the hiss of gasoline, bracing for impact, trying to save a life that is now his own.
